title.s: Adjective endings without an article (and a review)

grammar.explain:
You already know the adjective endings after **der, die, das** and after **ein, kein, mein** (A2). When there is **no article** at all, the adjective has to show the case and gender itself, so it takes the endings of the definite article: **der → -er, das → -es, die → -e, dem → -em, den → -en**: **kalter Tee, frisches Brot, frische Milch, mit kaltem Wasser, für heißen Tee**.
The only exception is the genitive masculine and neuter: there the adjective ends in **-en**, because the noun already shows the case with -s: **wegen schlechten Wetters**.
You need these endings with uncountable nouns (**Wasser, Brot, Wetter**), with plurals without an article (**alte Freunde, mit guten Freunden**), after numbers (**zwei kleine Kinder**) and after **viel, wenig, etwas**, which don't change themselves: **viel frisches Obst, mit etwas kaltem Wasser**. They are also typical of set phrases: **Liebe Grüße! Mit großer Freude …**
**Review – one simple rule:** the case must be shown once, either by the article or by the adjective.
• **der, die, das, dieser …:** the article shows the case, so the adjective only ends in **-e** or **-en**: **der alte Mann, mit dem alten Mann**.
• **ein, kein, mein …:** where the article has no ending (**ein** Mann, **ein** Haus), the adjective takes the strong ending: **ein alter Mann, ein kleines Haus**; everywhere else **-e** or **-en**: **einen alten Mann, in einem kleinen Haus**.
• **no article:** the adjective takes the strong ending: **alter Käse, frisches Brot, mit großer Freude**.

title.t: hinein, heraus, durch den Park, am Fluss entlang
title.s: Directions: hin and her, durch, entlang, gegenüber

grammar.explain:
**Wo?** asks about a position, **Wohin?** about a direction and **Woher?** about an origin. In speech, **wohin** and **woher** are often split: **Wo fährst du hin? Wo kommst du her?**
**hin** means movement **away from** the speaker, **her** movement **towards** the speaker. Combined with a preposition, they form separable prefixes for directions:
• **hinein – herein** (in), **hinaus – heraus** (out), **hinauf – herauf** (up), **hinunter – herunter** (down), **hinüber – herüber** (over, across)
**Komm herein!** (come in – towards me) – **Ich gehe hinaus.** (I'm going out – away from here). In everyday speech, both forms are usually shortened to **r-**: **rein, raus, rauf, runter, rüber**.
Three useful prepositions for routes and places:
• **durch + accusative** = through: **durch den Park, durch die Altstadt**
• **entlang** = along: usually **after** a noun in the accusative (**den Fluss entlang**) or as **an + dative … entlang** (**am Fluss entlang**). In written German you also find it before the noun with the genitive: **entlang des Flusses**.
• **gegenüber + dative** = opposite, across from: **gegenüber dem Bahnhof**, in speech often **gegenüber vom Bahnhof**. It follows a pronoun (**mir gegenüber**) and can also stand alone: **der Bäcker gegenüber** (the bakery across the street).
